passages.title: Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in isolated mitochondria
paragraphs: Mitochondria were isolated from rat liver and suspended in a buffered medium containing inorganic phosphate at pH 7.2 and 30 °C. Oxygen consumption was followed continuously with an oxygen electrode, and ATP synthesis was measured in parallel samples drawn from the same suspension. Rates were read from the linear part of each electrode trace over the minute that followed each addition, and normalised to the protein content of the preparation. Succinate, which donates electrons to the respiratory chain at complex II and so bypasses complex I, was supplied as the only oxidisable substrate. With succinate alone the suspension consumed oxygen slowly. The rate rose sharply when ADP was added and fell again once the added ADP had been converted to ATP. This dependence of respiration on the supply of ADP is called respiratory control, and the ratio of the ADP-stimulated rate to the resting rate is the respiratory control ratio.

Four further additions were tested. Oligomycin binds the ATP synthase and blocks proton flow through it. 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is a weak acid whose protonated form is lipid soluble: it crosses the inner membrane, releases a proton into the matrix, and returns as the anion. Cyanide binds complex IV. Each addition was made to a suspension that already contained succinate and 0.5 mM ADP, and the steady rates reached are given in Table 1.

In every condition in which ATP synthesis was abolished, the concentration of inorganic phosphate in the medium was unchanged at the end of the measurement, and mitochondria recovered from the cuvette still had an intact outer membrane. In a control given DNP without substrate, oxygen consumption was no faster than in the cyanide-treated sample, so the uncoupler does not itself donate electrons to the chain.

passages.title: Fat absorption in four subjects
paragraphs: Dietary triacylglycerol has to be hydrolysed before it can be absorbed. Pancreatic lipase, working with colipase at the surface of an emulsion droplet, removes the outer two fatty acids and leaves a 2-monoacylglycerol. Bile salts secreted into the duodenum disperse the emulsion and then carry the products in mixed micelles to the brush border of the enterocyte, where they are taken up. Inside the cell the fatty acids and the monoacylglycerol are re-esterified in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and the triacylglycerol so formed is packaged with apolipoprotein B-48 and phospholipid into a chylomicron. The chylomicron leaves across the basolateral membrane and enters the lymph, so chylomicron triacylglycerol appears in plasma an hour or two after a fatty meal.

Four subjects each ate a diet containing 100 g of fat per day for five days, and all faeces were collected and analysed for fat. On the sixth day each subject was given a standard fatty test meal, and the rise in plasma triacylglycerol above the fasting value was measured three hours later (Table 1). One of the four was a healthy control. Of the other three, one lacked pancreatic lipase, one had lost the terminal ileum and could not reclaim bile salts from the gut lumen, and one could not assemble chylomicrons. Which subject had which defect was not disclosed to the analysts.

Biopsies of the duodenal mucosa were taken four hours after the test meal. In one of the three affected subjects the enterocytes were swollen with large cytosolic lipid droplets; in the other two the mucosa looked normal under the microscope.

passages.title: Control of a mannitol catabolic operon
paragraphs: In the soil bacterium studied here, the three enzymes of mannitol catabolism are encoded by the mtl operon and transcribed as a single messenger RNA from one promoter. Immediately upstream of the promoter lies an operator. A separate gene, mtlR, sits elsewhere on the chromosome and encodes a protein, MtlR, that binds the operator as a dimer. Mannitol binds MtlR and lowers its affinity for the operator. A second site, further upstream of the promoter, is occupied by a complex of a small activator protein with cyclic AMP, and the concentration of cyclic AMP in these cells falls when glucose is available.

To measure transcription from the promoter, the investigators fused the promoter and operator to a reporter gene whose product is easy to assay, and introduced the fusion on a plasmid into four strains: the wild type, a strain carrying a deletion of mtlR, a strain carrying a single base substitution in the operator, and a strain carrying a single base substitution in mtlR. Each strain was grown in a minimal medium with glycerol as the carbon source. Reporter activity was measured after two hours in medium alone, in medium with 10 mM mannitol, and in medium with 10 mM mannitol and 10 mM glucose together (Table 1). Activity was assayed on permeabilised samples and expressed per unit of culture density at sampling, so the values do not depend on how many cells a culture contained.

All four strains grew at the same rate on glycerol, and in every strain the reporter plasmid was present at the same copy number, so differences in reporter activity reflect differences in transcription from the fused promoter. A plasmid lacking the promoter and operator gave no detectable activity in any medium.

passages.title: Two isoforms of a cell-surface receptor
paragraphs: The receptor studied here is encoded by a gene of eight exons. Exon 6, which is 144 nucleotides long, encodes the single transmembrane segment. Exon 5, immediately upstream of it, is 108 nucleotides long and encodes part of the extracellular stalk. Two mature messenger RNAs are made from the same pre-messenger RNA. In form A every exon is retained and the protein is anchored in the plasma membrane. In form B exon 6 is skipped, exon 5 being joined directly to exon 7; the reading frame is preserved across the new junction, and the protein that results is released into the medium. Both forms use the same promoter, the same transcription start site and the same polyadenylation site.

Inclusion of exon 6 depends on a serine- and arginine-rich splicing factor that binds a short sequence inside exon 6 and recruits the spliceosome to the weak upstream splice site. Cultured cells were left untreated, treated for 12 hours with an inflammatory cytokine, transfected with a small interfering RNA against the splicing factor, or transfected with a plasmid that overexpresses the factor. The two messenger RNAs were then measured by reverse transcription and quantitative PCR. In untreated cells 85% of receptor transcripts were form A; after the cytokine, 40% were form A; after knockdown of the splicing factor, 20%; and after overexpression of the factor, 95%. In each condition the rest of the transcripts were form B.

Total receptor messenger RNA, measured with a primer pair lying in exons 2 and 3, fell between 97 and 102 arbitrary units in all four conditions. The amount of receptor pre-messenger RNA, measured with a primer pair spanning the junction between exon 4 and the intron that follows it, differed between conditions by less than 10%.

passages.title: Three viruses compared in one cell line
paragraphs: Three viruses that grow in the same cultured mammalian cell line were compared. Virus P has a single-stranded RNA genome of positive sense and no envelope, and completes its cycle in the cytoplasm. Virus Q is enveloped, carries two copies of a single-stranded RNA genome, and packages a polymerase that copies RNA into DNA; the DNA product is inserted into a host chromosome before any viral messenger RNA is made. Virus R has a double-stranded DNA genome and replicates in the nucleus. Yields of infectious virus were measured 24 hours after infection by plaque assay and are reported as the common logarithm of plaque-forming units per millilitre (Table 1).

Four treatments were applied one hour before infection and maintained throughout. A nucleoside analogue that is accepted by RNA-dependent DNA polymerases and terminates the growing chain was used at 10 micromolar. Actinomycin D was used at a concentration that blocks host DNA-dependent RNA polymerases without killing the cells within 24 hours. Cycloheximide blocks the elongation step of translation on host ribosomes. A peptide inhibitor of the Virus P protease was used at 5 micromolar.

In a separate experiment, genomic nucleic acid was purified free of protein from each virus and introduced into uninfected cells by transfection. Virus P RNA and Virus R DNA each gave rise to infectious virus; purified Virus Q RNA gave none that could be detected.

In a third experiment, cells were held outside the division cycle by withdrawing serum for 48 hours before infection. Under those conditions the yield of Virus R fell by two logarithms while the yield of Virus P was unchanged. In the Virus R cultures the proportion of cells that had replicated their DNA rose from 3% at the time of infection to 45% eighteen hours later, and no such rise was seen in uninfected cultures kept without serum alongside them.

passages.title: Filling, contractility and cardiac output
paragraphs: In an anaesthetised large-animal preparation, left ventricular volume was measured by an imaging method at the end of diastole and at the end of systole, and heart rate was recorded at the same time. Stroke volume is the difference between the two volumes; cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate; and the ejection fraction is the stroke volume expressed as a fraction of the end-diastolic volume. Four conditions were studied in the same animal, in the order shown in Table 1, with at least 30 minutes between them and with measurements taken only once the circulation had settled. Each volume was taken as the mean of five consecutive beats recorded during a short pause in ventilation, and the imaging planes were set once at baseline and not moved between conditions.

The first condition was the untreated baseline. The second was produced by rapid infusion of warmed saline into a central vein, which raises venous return without acting directly on the myocardium. The third was produced by infusing a drug that increases the amount of calcium delivered to the myofilaments with each beat; this drug also acts on the sinoatrial node. The fourth followed a single dose of a beta-adrenergic antagonist. Mean arterial pressure was held within 10 mmHg of the baseline value throughout by adjusting a clamp on the aorta, so the load against which the ventricle ejected was similar in all four conditions. Body temperature and arterial oxygen saturation were held near baseline in every condition.

No arrhythmia was recorded at any point, and the ventricular wall was reported to thicken normally during systole in every condition, so the measured volumes reflect ordinary contraction rather than regional failure of the muscle.

passages.title: A three-point cross in a flour beetle
paragraphs: Three recessive mutations affecting body colour, antenna shape and wing texture were followed in a flour beetle, and are written b, a and c in that arbitrary order. A female beetle whose two homologues carried b, a and c together on one chromosome and the three wild-type alleles together on the other was crossed to a male homozygous for all three recessive alleles. Because the male can contribute only recessive alleles, the phenotype of each offspring reveals directly which combination of alleles it received from its mother. One thousand offspring were scored, and the combination each of them received from the mother is given in Table 1. The three genes lie close enough together that no triple crossover is expected in a sample of this size.

A map distance is defined as the percentage of gametes in which an exchange occurred between the two genes concerned, and one map unit, or centimorgan, is one per cent recombination. Offspring in which an exchange occurred in each of the two intervals carry an exchange in both, and so must be counted in both intervals when the distances are worked out. If exchanges in the two intervals occurred independently of one another, the expected frequency of double-crossover gametes would be the product of the two interval frequencies.

A plus sign in Table 1 stands for the wild-type allele of the gene in that position. The eight classes together account for all 1000 offspring scored, and no offspring was excluded from the count. All three phenotypes were scored on adults under a dissecting microscope by two observers working independently, and the few beetles on which they disagreed were re-examined before being assigned to a class.

passages.title: A steroid and a peptide hormone compared
paragraphs: Cultured liver cells were used to compare the action of a synthetic steroid, S, with that of a peptide hormone, P. S is a small hydrophobic molecule. Its receptor is a protein with four separable parts: a hydrophobic pocket that binds the hormone, a zinc-coordinating module that binds a particular DNA sequence, a short stretch of basic residues recognised by the machinery that imports proteins into the nucleus, and a surface that recruits coactivators. P binds a receptor in the plasma membrane and raises cytosolic cyclic AMP within seconds. Both hormones increase transcription of the same target gene, and a reporter carrying that gene's regulatory region was used to follow the response.

Four variants of the experiment were run with steroid S. In the first, actinomycin D was present throughout. In the second, the cells expressed a receptor in which the stretch of basic residues had been replaced by alanines; this protein bound S normally and bound the DNA sequence normally when both were tested in vitro. In the third, S was coupled covalently to a 70 kDa polymer that cannot cross a lipid bilayer, and the conjugate bound the purified receptor with the same affinity as free S. Values in Table 1 are fold changes in reporter messenger RNA relative to untreated cells, measured at three times after the hormone was added.

Untreated cells contained about 400 copies of the reporter messenger RNA per cell. Cell viability was above 95% in every condition at the end of the eight hours, and the amount of a housekeeping transcript measured alongside the reporter varied by less than 5% between conditions.

passages.title: Exit of a secreted enzyme from the cell
paragraphs: A secreted enzyme was studied in a cultured cell line. Its messenger RNA encodes a polypeptide of 54.5 kDa, of which the first 2.5 kDa is a hydrophobic signal sequence removed by a protease in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum. The remaining chain carries two sites at which an oligosaccharide can be attached to the amide nitrogen of an asparagine side chain. Each oligosaccharide is added in the endoplasmic reticulum as a core of about 2 kDa and is then extended during passage through the Golgi apparatus, so the mature secreted form is larger than the form found in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Cells were labelled with radioactive amino acids for ten minutes and then chased with unlabelled medium. Labelled protein was recovered from the cells and from the medium after two hours, and its apparent mass was measured on a denaturing gel. Five preparations were compared: cells expressing the wild-type enzyme; cells expressing a construct from which the codons for the signal sequence had been deleted; wild-type cells treated with tunicamycin, which blocks the first step in the assembly of asparagine-linked oligosaccharides; cells expressing a construct in which both asparagine codons had been changed to glutamine; and wild-type cells treated with brefeldin A. Results are given in Table 1. Apparent mass was read against a set of marker proteins run in the same gel, and each mass in Table 1 is the mean of three independent chases, which agreed to within 1 kDa.
Total incorporation of label into protein differed between the five preparations by less than 8%, and none of the treatments reduced cell viability below 95% over the two hours of the chase.

passages.title: Two routes to the same lesion
paragraphs: Complement can be activated either by antibody bound to a target surface or by a route that needs no antibody at all. In the antibody-dependent route, C1q recognises bound antibody and activates associated proteases, which cleave C4 and C2 to build a C3 convertase. In the antibody-independent route, a small amount of C3b deposited spontaneously on a surface binds factor B; cleavage of factor B yields a second kind of C3 convertase, which deposits more C3b and so amplifies the response. Both routes converge on the cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b, then on the cleavage of C5, after which C6, C7, C8 and several molecules of C9 assemble in the target membrane as the pore that lyses the cell.

Serum from four patients and from a healthy donor was tested in two assays. In the first, target cells coated with antibody were incubated with serum and lysis was measured; this assay reports the activity of the antibody-dependent route. In the second, serum was diluted into a buffer that excludes the calcium the antibody-dependent route requires, then incubated with a surface that activates the antibody-independent route, and lysis was measured again. Serum C3 was measured separately, and the reference interval in this laboratory is 100 to 180 mg/dL. Each patient was subsequently shown to have a complete deficiency of one complement protein.

In both assays, heating a serum sample to 56 °C for 30 minutes before use abolished lysis entirely, including in the healthy donor's serum, which confirms that the lysis measured depended on heat-labile serum proteins rather than on the target cells themselves.
